terms.meaning: the part of the app that decides how to answer a question using the documents
a match when a piece of text appears anywhere inside another
a check of how well an answer meets expected results

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and path setup
sections.what: Loads the test helpers, adds the backend folder to Python's search path, and loads the agent and logger.
sections.why: The backend folder is not an installed package, so the path must be added by hand.
sections.watch_out: Importing the agent loads the full question-answering system, so this script needs the same keys and packages as the app.

sections.name: ExcelTestRunner (part 1)
sections.title: Setting up the runner and reading the test sheet
sections.what: Creates a runner for an Excel file and a collection, builds the agent, and reads the spreadsheet, requiring a question column. Optional columns are expected_files, expected_keywords and notes.
sections.why: Lets testers write questions in Excel without touching code.
sections.watch_out: The agent is built when the runner is created, so the model and database must be ready before any test is read.

sections.name: ExcelTestRunner: run_test_case
sections.title: Running one question and scoring it
sections.what: Sends one question to the agent and records the answer, source file names, confidence and evidence count. If the sheet lists expected files or keywords, it also reports which were found, which were missed, and a match rate for each.
sections.why: Lets testers compare answers against what they expected.
sections.watch_out: Keyword matching is a simple lowercase substring check, so a word inside another word counts as a match.

sections.name: ExcelTestRunner (part 3)
sections.title: Finishing error handling and running all tests
sections.what: Ends the error handling for a single test, then runs every row of the Excel test sheet one at a time and collects each result. After that, it starts building the final report by counting total, successful and failed tests, and averaging how well the file names and keywords matched the expected answers.
sections.why: Likely reason: each test is run in turn and the results are gathered in one list so the report can summarize them together. Reason not stated in the code for using 0 as the average when no rates exist.
sections.watch_out: Results that have no match rate, such as errors, are silently left out of the averages, so an average can look healthy even when many tests failed.

sections.name: ExcelTestRunner (part 4)
sections.title: Saving the JSON and Excel reports
sections.what: Counts how many answers were rated high, medium or low confidence, then bundles the totals and every individual result into one report. It saves that report as a JSON file and also writes an Excel workbook with a Results sheet and a Summary sheet, so the owner can review it in a spreadsheet.
sections.why: Likely reason: JSON is kept for programs to read and Excel is added so a person can review results easily, as the inline comment says.
sections.watch_out: The Excel file name is made by swapping the text ".json" in the output path, so an output path without ".json" would make the Excel file overwrite the JSON report.

sections.name: ExcelTestRunner: print_summary
sections.title: Printing a short summary to the screen
sections.what: Prints a boxed summary in the terminal showing total tests, successful tests, failed tests and the success rate as a percentage. If there are no results, it prints a short message saying so instead.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives the person running the tests a quick result without opening the report files.
sections.watch_out: The success rate is calculated from the same results list, so it only reflects tests that finished; if the run stopped early, the percentage describes only the tests that ran.

sections.name: main
sections.title: Command line entry for running tests
sections.what: Reads the Excel file path from the command line, plus optional settings for the collection to query (default "default") and the report output location (default test_results/report.json). It then runs all tests, saves the report and prints the summary.
sections.why: Lets the owner start a full test run from a terminal with one command, without editing the code.
sections.watch_out: Steps run in order, so if generating the report fails with an error, the summary printed afterwards will not appear.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Starting point when run directly
sections.what: Runs the command line function only when this file is launched directly as a program. If another file imports this one, nothing runs automatically.
sections.why: Standard Python pattern so the test code can be reused by other files without starting a test run.

summary: Runs questions listed in an Excel sheet against the question-answering agent and scores the answers against expected files and keywords.
purpose: Lets testers check answer quality with a spreadsheet, without writing code.
why: Likely reason: testers can add cases in Excel and get a repeatable report.
how: The script adds the backend folder to the search path and creates the agent. It reads the spreadsheet, requiring a question column. For each row it asks the agent, then checks the source file names and answer keywords against the optional columns and records the match rates. Results are summarised and written to reports.
inputs: An Excel file with a question column and optional expected_files, expected_keywords and notes columns, a collection name, and the agent's own settings and keys.
outputs: A list of result records per question, a printed summary, and report files in the test_results folder.
risks: Keyword checks are simple substring matches, so partial words count. The runner needs live model and database access, so results can change between runs. Exact file name matching misses files listed with a different path.
debug: If the sheet fails to load, check the question column name. If every case fails, check the agent setup and keys in settings. If keyword results look wrong, check for partial matches.
